summary: Sea Cliff arrived as somebody's subdivision and was handed over to the city piece by piece: a bond posted in 1916 against the unpaid taxes on Subdivision No. 2, deeds to its streets accepted in 1923, a map approved in 1926 extending Lake Street out to Camino del Mar and opening Sea View Terrace. The sewer down California Street was paid for in 1906, before most of the houses existed, and the avenues between California and Lake were curbed and paved one at a time after that, with an arc lamp at the corner. Once the houses arrived the commonest record by far became a fuel-oil tank going in under one of them — fifteen hundred gallons at 2975 Lake Street, fifteen hundred at 2801, two hundred and fifty at the corner of Twenty-seventh and California. What the Board mostly did besides that was decide how far back from the street a house had to stand — five feet along one length of Twenty-seventh Avenue and ten along the next, ten on Thirty-second, where Joseph Novitsky filed an objection — and which of the two residential zones each corner belonged in. The Bergerot School went up on Twenty-fifth Avenue in 1908 for $37,000, and sixteen years later the Board of Education asked to rope off Twenty-fourth Avenue behind it during the recess hour. Underneath runs the sewer that carries the whole district: by 1939 a control gate at Twenty-fourth Avenue and Lake Street was holding the Richmond's flow to eighteen million gallons a day. In 1932 Villamar Avenue was renamed Twenty-fifth Avenue North, and four years later its front doors were renumbered to match. After that the record thins to almost nothing — a condominium map now and then, an argument in 2020 over a house on Seacliff Avenue, and in 2022 the naming of the old City Cemetery that lies under Lincoln Park.
